originalTitle: Bill Miller's investing strategy: How the legendary fund manager outperformed the market for 15 straight years
simplifiedContent: Bill Miller, a well-known investor, was able to do better than the overall stock market for 15 years in a row. He achieved this by using a strategy that involves looking for stocks that are undervalued, being patient, and not following the crowd. Miller's approach focuses on finding the true worth of a company, its ability to generate cash, and buying stocks when they are safe and cheap. This strategy allowed him to make good investments by taking advantage of times when the market overreacted and selling stocks when they reached a fair price. By doing so, Miller was able to outperform the market consistently over a long period of time.

originalTitle: Utkarsh Small Finance Bank posts Rs 34 crore Q1 loss; asset quality stress persists
simplifiedContent: Utkarsh Small Finance Bank recently reported a loss of Rs 34 crore for the first quarter of the year. This is the fifth quarter in a row that the bank has lost money. The bank's performance is being hurt by "asset quality stress", which means that many of the loans it has given out are not being paid back. The bank's loss is smaller than it was before, but it still has a lot of bad loans, with 6.1% of its total loans not being paid back. This news matters because it shows that the bank is still struggling with some major problems.

originalTitle: Muthoot Finance reports 25% rise in Q1 profit, announces leadership transition
simplifiedContent: Muthoot Finance, a company that lends money to people using their gold as security, made a profit of Rs 2,550 crore in the first quarter of the year. This is 25% more than they made in the same quarter last year. The company's profit increased because its gold loan business is doing well. The company is also changing its leadership, with Alexander George Muthoot taking over as managing director starting October 1, if the company's shareholders agree. This news matters because it shows how well the company is performing and who will be in charge of making important decisions in the future.

originalTitle: Yen Traders Brace for More Intervention With US at Japan’s Side
simplifiedContent: Here's what's happening: Japan and the US worked together last week to try to strengthen the Japanese yen, and now traders are waiting to see if they'll do it again. This means that Japan and the US took actions to try to increase the value of the yen compared to other currencies. The traders are paying close attention because this could affect the value of the yen again, and they want to be prepared. This is important because it can impact investing and trading in the markets, especially for people who deal with the yen. The traders will be watching closely on Monday to see what happens next.

originalTitle: Wall Street’s Favorite Bet Comes Undone as Chips Whipsaw Market
simplifiedContent: Here's what's happening in simple terms: there's been a big trend in the stock market this year where investors have been betting heavily on companies that make semiconductors, also known as "chips". This trend is now starting to reverse, which is causing a lot of volatility in the market. Volatility means that stock prices are moving up and down quickly, which can be unsettling for investors. This is happening because investors are getting worried that companies won't keep spending as much on artificial intelligence, which has been driving the demand for semiconductors. This change is significant because it could affect the overall direction of the stock market.

originalTitle: Banks Offload Risk from Leveraged ETFs With Exotic ‘Crash Puts’
simplifiedContent: There are investment products called leveraged ETFs that promise to multiply the daily returns of a stock, but they are very risky for investors. To manage this risk, banks are using a special tool called "crash puts". This means that banks are trying to protect themselves from potential big losses. This matters because it shows that even banks think these investment products are very risky. By using "crash puts", banks are trying to offload some of this risk, which could help prevent big losses if something goes wrong.
